Question: Tamika selects two different numbers at random from the set \(\{8,9,10\}\) and adds them. Carlos takes two different numbers at random from the set \(\{3,5,6\}\) and multiplies them. What is the probability that Tamika’s result is greater than Carlos’ result?
Solution:
Order does not affect either result, so list each pair of different numbers only once. Tamika's pairs \((8,9),(8,10),(9,10)\) give sums \(17,18,19\). Carlos's pairs \((3,5),(3,6),(5,6)\) give products \(15,18,30\).

Each person's three pairs are equally likely: each pair can be selected in two orders. Their independent selections therefore give \(3\times3=9\) equally likely combinations, one for every sum paired with every product.

The winning comparisons, written as \((\text{Tamika's result},\text{Carlos's result})\), are exactly
\[
(17,15),\quad(18,15),\quad(19,15),\quad(19,18).
\]
No sum exceeds \(30\), and the tie \((18,18)\) does not count. These are four distinct favorable outcomes among nine, so the probability is \(\boxed{\frac49}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
